title: Smallholding first aid kit essentials
subtitle: What to keep in the shed for common livestock emergencies before the vet arrives.
excerpt: A well-stocked first aid kit in the livestock shed lets you stabilise a sick or injured animal before a vet arrives, and handle routine minor procedures without a call-out. The contents differ between species, but a core kit covers the most common emergencies across sheep, goats, pigs, poultry, and rabbits. Here is what belongs in a small holding first aid kit.
sourceNotes: NADIS, Emergency First Aid for Farm Animals. AHDB, farm animal health guidance. RSPCA, livestock emergency guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: Prescription-only veterinary medicines, available only on written prescription from a veterinary surgeon. Antibiotics, certain vaccines, and some analgesics in the UK are POM-V. They cannot legally be purchased or administered without a prescription from a vet who has examined the animal.

content.text: A first aid kit cannot replace a vet. It contains the items that stabilise an animal in the 30 to 120 minutes before a vet can attend, and the supplies for routine minor work that does not require
. Keep the kit in a waterproof box, clearly labelled, in a consistent location everyone on the holding knows.
Clinical thermometer (digital): normal range varies by species. Sheep and goats: 38.5 to 39.5°C. Pigs: 38.5 to 39.5°C. Poultry: 40.5 to 42°C. Rabbits: 38.5 to 39.5°C.
Latex gloves (box of 100): for any internal examination, wound treatment, or lambing assistance.
Sterile saline sachets or a bottle of sterile wound wash: for cleaning cuts and eye injuries.
Wound spray (antiseptic): protects surface wounds and deters flies.
Bandage roll and self-adhesive bandage (cohesive): for leg wounds and splints.
Sterile gauze pads: for wound dressings and pressure on bleeding wounds.
Rehydration salts: for scouring lambs and sick animals that cannot drink enough on their own.
Stomach tube and 60 ml syringe: for administering liquids to a very weak lamb or kid that cannot suckle.
Sheep and goats: colostrum supplement for orphan or weak lambs, lamb stomach tube and bottle. Ask your vet about holding a supply of injectable calcium for emergencies.
Pigs: liquid paraffin (for constipation in sows post-farrowing), heat lamp or heat mat for chilled piglets.
Poultry: crop needle for blockages, flystrike prevention spray, and an isolation box with bedding.
What to include from your vet

Discuss with your vet what prescription items they are willing to supply for your emergency kit. A good relationship usually means a small supply of antibiotics, pain relief, and calcium can be held at the holding under a written prescription. Inspect and replace kit items annually; check expiry dates on medicines and replace saline sachets if the seal is broken.
